title: Microsoft, Nvidia push provenance checks as open-weight AI adoption accelerates
raw_text: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said . “Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.” The framework covers cybersecurity, data protection, content, human-AI interaction, and bias. Its cybersecurity category includes malicious code generation, malicious tool calls, extraction of the model’s safety policies, excessive token generation, and behavior that diverges from the intended system goal. The paper draws on existing NIST and ISO risk-management standards and is the first in a planned series on managing risks across open-weight AI deployments, the companies said in a blog post. Model changes can weaken safeguards Open-weight models can be fine-tuned, merged with other models, modified, or repackaged for different uses. But those changes can weaken a model’s safety protections even when it continues to perform its intended task well, Microsoft and Nvidia said. “Safety behaviors are often the more fragile of the two,” the companies wrote. Changes to model weights, fine-tuning, quantization and configuration can “degrade safeguards while leaving task performance intact.” That creates a challenge for enterprise security teams: a model may continue to deliver accurate results on routine tasks even after changes have affected how it responds to unsafe requests. The companies advise enterprises to assess safety and capability separately, test the specific model configuration they intend to deploy, and repeat evaluations after significant changes. “No volume of behavioral testing establishes what an artifact is, only how it behaves,” the paper said. It recommends using cryptographic signatures to verify that a model matches the publisher’s original artifact. “Where signatures are unavailable, record the unverified integrity as an open risk rather than treating evaluation results as closing it,” the paper recommended. For enterprises, Gartner recommends independent adversarial testing, static scanning of model files, and provenance verification before and after deployment. Gartner’s proposed vetting process also calls for verifying model sources, checking file integrity, conducting adversarial testing, and recording approved models in an enterprise registry. Security must extend beyond the model Microsoft and Nvidia caution that evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of the application built around it. “Model evaluation alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application; enterprises must also assess permissions, data access, connected tools, runtime behavior, and operational controls,” the paper says. The guidance recommends assessing models in their intended operating context and maintaining controls across the model, runtime, harness, and application layers. It also calls for monitoring model inputs, outputs, and tool use after deployment. According to Gartner, open-weight model traffic must be routed through governed AI gateways to enforce authentication, prompt-injection defenses, sensitive-data protection and audit logging. The research firm also recommends isolating self-hosted runtimes and applying controls suited to other deployment models, including private network paths and customer-managed encryption keys for cloud API consumption. Gartner reported that client inquiries about open-weight models through its research inquiry service rose by more than 30% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the first quarter. The firm projects that open-weight models will account for 50% of enterprise AI use cases by 2028, up from 20% at the time of its report. Staffing and accountability matter Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said self-hosting requires enterprises to account for the people and processes needed to maintain safeguards. “Self-hosting is a staffing decision as much as an infrastructure one, and the people to carry it must move with the model,” Gogia said. He cautioned against assuming that self-hosting necessarily means replacing all the safeguards available through managed services. In his assessment, a significant gap can be the provider’s misuse-investigation function, while customer responsibilities depend on the service and its configuration. Gogia said the Microsoft-Nvidia paper provides useful guidance but leaves important areas for future work. The authors say subsequent publications will extend risk-management guidance across the runtime, harness, and application layers. “The sharper question is who is contractually obliged to re-test and patch the model when a new stripping technique lands,” Gogia said. For CISOs, Gogia recommends assessing the model, deployment, and intended use before approving production workloads. He also advises security teams to retain control of their risk registers rather than relying exclusively on a vendor-developed taxonomy.
summary: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said .

title: ConnectWise backup credentials exposed multiple Microsoft 365 tenants
raw_text: ConnectWise has disabled key cloud services and is investigating unauthorized access to customers’ Microsoft 365 environments after a credential tied to its Cloud Backup platform was compromised and used to authenticate into customer tenants, prompting Huntress to identify suspicious sign-ins across 162 organizations. The activity involved the Cloud Backup application obtaining Microsoft Graph access tokens using a credential associated with ConnectWise’s own tenant. Security firm Huntress has also confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 19:00 UTC on October 16. Huntress said the application authenticated from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06.13 and 08.34 UTC. The address belonged to a hosting provider, rather than the Azure private IP space from which the application normally communicated. The authentication events were recorded in Microsoft’s sign-in logs. ConnectWise has acknowledged the activity and has disabled seven application identities on October 17. It also suspended Cloud Backup, along with SaaS Security and Cloud Management. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company updated its advisory on October 19 and said it had not observed successful threat activity in the environments it monitors since implementing containment measures, but had yet to establish a timeline for restoring the services. “Existing backup archives remain encrypted and isolated, and we have no indication that those archives have been compromised,” noted ConnectWise. The October 19 advisory update included two additional IP addresses, 144.172.64[.]99 and 144.172.64[.]60, identified through downstream security monitoring. Integration credentials used to escalate access ConnectWise Cloud Backup needs broad permissions to back up and restore customer data across Microsoft 365 services, including Exchange Online, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams. Huntress said the compromised credential allowed the application to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants without requiring an individual user to sign in. That application-based authentication does not involve a user password or trigger the multi-factor authentication ( MFA ) prompt associated with a usual login. The credential lives in the vendor’s own environment, meaning customers could not have generated it through activity in their individual tenants. Huntress also identified activity involving a second ConnectWise application, Cloud Management for Microsoft Teams, in one partner tenant. According to the security firm, the application assigned itself the Global Administrator role and added credentials to two other applications, including a Huntress application specific to that partner. The sequence took approximately five minutes, Huntress said, adding that it had not established whether the separate stages of activity were conducted by the same operator. Service suspensions buy time, but tenant-level checks remain necessary ConnectWise disabled the seven application identities and revoked certificates associated with affected application connections. The company said those actions prevent new authentication through the disabled connections but do not automatically reverse changes already made inside customer tenants. Previously issued access tokens may also remain usable until they expire or are otherwise invalidated, it added. The service disruption extends beyond backups. With Cloud Backup suspended, scheduled backups, access to affected archives, and restoration capabilities remain unavailable. SaaS Security monitoring and alerting, as well as Cloud Management’s user and license management functions, have also been taken offline while remediation continues. Huntress said its investigation had not confirmed data theft. In the one tenant whose audit logs it examined in detail, the firm found no recorded mail or file access, but warned that this did not prove that no data had been taken. Some Microsoft Graph directory reads do not leave an audit trail, limiting what investigators can establish from available records, it noted. Both companies have urged partners and customer administrators to review their Microsoft 365 environments. ConnectWise’s guidance calls for checks of application sign-ins, credentials, directory roles, consent grants, policy changes, and possible mailbox forwarding or other persistence mechanisms. ConnectWise partners were also advised to keep affected applications disabled until it provides formal restoration instructions. As of October 19, investigation and service restoration efforts remained ongoing.

The activity involved the Cloud Backup application obtaining Microsoft Graph access tokens using a credential associated with ConnectWise’s own tenant. Security firm Huntress has also confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 19:00 UTC on October 16. title: The password nobody owns: Taking machines to zero standing privilege (ZSP)
raw_text: Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands. Multiply that across the landscape, and the numbers get uncomfortable quickly. Palo Alto Networks surveyed more than 2,900 security leaders for its 2026 Identity Security Landscape and found an average of 109 machine identities for every human one. I’d treat any single ratio with some caution, since each vendor counts identities differently. The same report’s finding that 61% of privileged access requests are still met with standing privilege, instead of being granted on demand, is much harder to wave away. Entro Labs looked at the age of these identities too. Close to half were more than a year old, and 7.5% had been around for somewhere between five and ten years. Over the past decade, most security programmes have put real effort into controlling human admins through PAM. Machine accounts tended to get a vault and a rotation schedule, and in most of the programmes I’ve worked on, that’s roughly where the effort on them ended. Why rotation only buys you time Vaulting and rotating a service account password beats leaving it hard-coded in a script, and I wouldn’t advise anyone to pull out a vault that’s working. Rotation changes the secret, though it leaves the access exactly as it was. Between one change and the next, the credential stays valid with every permission intact, readable from wherever the application fetches it. If an attacker copies it a few days into a ninety-day cycle, they’ve got close to three months to use it quietly. OAuth integrations make this worse, because a refresh token can keep renewing itself long after anyone remembers granting it. The Salesloft Drift campaign in August 2025 is the clearest recent example I can point to. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that the actor it tracks as UNC6395 used stolen OAuth and refresh tokens tied to the Drift integration to pull data out of Salesforce customer instances between 8 and 18 August, and more than 700 organisations were caught up in it. Because the tokens were genuine and no person was signing in, there was no MFA prompt to trip and nothing unusual for the authentication layer to notice. I suspect plenty of the affected customers would have struggled to name who in their own team had approved that integration in the first place. I’d want every CIO to look closely at what the attackers were after. Customers were told to search their Salesforce records for secrets such as AWS keys and Snowflake tokens, since support cases are a common place for staff to paste credentials while troubleshooting. In other words, the stolen standing token was being used to hunt for more standing tokens in other systems. Salesloft later linked the initial access to a compromise of its GitHub account back in March, months before the theft began. width="1024" height="469" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Figure 1: Standing credential vs zero standing privilege . Ashish Mishra What zero standing privilege looks like for a machine With zero standing privilege, a machine identity holds no usable access while it sits idle. When it has work to do, it proves who it is to a policy engine and gets back a short-lived credential scoped to that job, which expires on its own once the job finishes. Most of you will already have something like this for people, usually as just-in-time elevation through a PAM platform. Workloads tend to get there through workload identity federation instead. The workload presents a signed token from a platform the target already trusts, such as a Kubernetes cluster or a CI pipeline, and swaps it for temporary access. GitHub Actions deploying into AWS is the easiest case to picture. The pipeline requests an OIDC token from GitHub, AWS checks it against a trust policy tied to that repository, and the job runs under a role whose credentials last around an hour by default. No access key gets stored in the repo at any point. Google’s own authentication action for GitHub recommends federation over exported service account keys on the same grounds, warning that those keys are long-lived and need the same care as a password. Getting there without breaking production Full zero standing privilege across every machine identity isn’t achievable in most enterprises right now, and it’s worth saying so plainly to your board. Older applications that log in to a database with a username and password won’t federate, and plenty of vendor appliances only accept a static API key. Practitioners increasingly describe near-zero standing privilege as the realistic target for machines, which is how I’d frame it too. Everything starts with an inventory. You need every machine credential in one place, including the OAuth grants your SaaS integrations hold, with a named human owner recorded against each. The owner field can look like admin overhead, but an account with no owner tends to survive every clean-up exercise, because nobody has the authority to approve switching it off. Once the list exists, sort it by what an attacker could reach with each credential. CI/CD pipelines and cloud admin roles usually end up near the top, and they also happen to be where federation is most mature, so moving pipelines to OIDC tends to be one of the earliest wins. Connected SaaS apps deserve a separate look. A lot of them were approved years ago with broad scopes, often by a business team rather than security, and nobody has revisited them since. Cut the scopes down to what each integration actually uses. It’s also fair to ask suppliers how they store the refresh tokens they hold on your behalf, and after Drift, a vendor with access to your CRM should have a ready answer. Some systems won’t federate for years. In those cases, you can still shorten how long a credential lives, even if you can’t change what it’s allowed to do. Vault-issued dynamic secrets work well here, with the database account created when the session starts and dropped when it closes, and the application usually needs little or no rewriting. For board reporting, the number I’d track is the share of machine access granted on demand compared with the share held permanently. Expect the first reading to look poor. It’s still worth putting in front of the board early, since the change from one quarter to the next tells them far more about progress than any single snapshot.
summary: Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands. Multiply that across the landscape, and the numbers get uncomfortable quickly.

title: 9 rising malware trends every security pro should know
raw_text: Malware is evolving rapidly, driven by advances in AI and changes in computing infrastructures. Security professionals must continuously educate themselves on these trends to defend against increasingly sophisticated threats. The traditional game of cat and mouse between security attackers and defenders has got fiercer with fresh techniques evolving and older less effective approaches falling out of fashion. Here is a look at what’s heating up in the world of malware — and what’s cooling off. Infostealers commoditizing initial access Infostealers have experienced huge growth in the past 18 months, with malware such as Lumma Stealer , StealC, and RisePro now responsible for 75% of all stolen credentials, according to cybersecurity vendor Immersive. Infostealers steal browser cookies, VPN credentials, multi-factor authentication (MFA) tokens, crypto wallet data, and more. Cybercriminals sell the data that infostealers grab through dark web markets , giving attackers easy access to corporate systems. “This shift commoditizes initial access, enabling nation-state goals through simple transactions rather than complex attacks,” says Ben McCarthy, lead cyber security engineer at Immersive. Malicious packages targeting developer environments Threat actors are systematically compromising the software supply chain by embedding malicious code within legitimate development tools, libraries, and frameworks that organizations use to build applications. “These supply chain attacks exploit the trust between developers and package repositories,” Immersive’s McCarthy tells CSO. “Malicious packages often mimic legitimate ones while running harmful code, evading standard code reviews.” Popular software development ecosystems such as NPM , PyPI , and AI platforms like HuggingFace are frequent targets of malicious actors seeking to seed compromised packages in software developers’ toolchains. Attackers continued to innovate in 2026 when targeting the software supply chain as a vector for malware delivery. For example, the Shai-Hulud attacks involved self-propagating malware that stole CI/CD secrets and hijacked GitHub Actions OIDC tokens to publish malicious package versions through victims’ own release pipelines. Similar tactics were in play in other attacks. “In the Axios compromise , attackers targeted the lead maintainer’s credentials and inserted a malicious dependency into legitimate software releases,” says Lindsey O’Donnell-Welch, principal technical writer at managed detection and response firm Huntress. “This led to downstream dependencies downloading remote-access malware tailored to the operating system.” Ransomware becoming more targeted and sophisticated The ransomware landscape shifted dramatically after law enforcement cracked down on major groups like LockBit. Modern ransomware threat actors such as RansomHub and Akira now favor smaller, highly targeted attacks, using ransomware as a final step after full infiltration and data exfiltration. This marks a move from broad, opportunistic strikes to focused, high-value campaigns. “These targeted approaches show threat actors’ growing insight into specific vulnerabilities and their readiness to invest heavily in reconnaissance and tailored attack development,” Immersive’s McCarthy comments. These groups use advanced evasion techniques such as living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics and legitimate admin tools to stay hidden. They’re also shifting from file encryption to data theft and extortion, threatening public leaks to pressure victims. “There’s been a notable uptick in the use of cloud-based services and remote management platforms as part of ransomware toolchains,” says Jamie Moles, senior technical marketing manager at network detection and response provider ExtraHop. “This aligns with a broader trend: Rather than relying solely on traditional malware payloads, adversaries are increasingly shifting toward abusing trusted platforms and ‘living-off-the-land’ techniques.” Healthcare remains a top target of ransomware attacks , while critical infrastructure faces increasing threats as attackers exploit the urgency that prompts quick ransom payments. Malware adopting social engineering techniques Cybercriminals are increasingly adopting ClickFix as a malware delivery method in attacks that rely on social engineering techniques to successfully infect end-user devices. ClickFix tricks users into executing malicious code — usually a PowerShell script — on their own systems, taking advantage of growing user fatigue in having to jump through online hoops to ‘prove you’re human.’ By hijacking trust in familiar CAPTCHA processes, threat actors are getting users to actively participate in their own compromise — copying and pasting malicious commands into their systems under the guise of simple verification. “We’ve seen this technique gain serious traction across phishing sites, compromised webpages, and social engineering campaigns,” says Jim Walter, senior threat researcher at SentinelLABS. “It’s simple, effective, and increasingly common.” CISOs need to be wary of the threat because it bypasses many traditional detection methods by relying on human behavior rather than system vulnerabilities. “Raising awareness, hardening endpoint execution policies, and deploying behavioral detection tools are essential to countering this wave of malware delivery,” Walter advises. Threat actors continue to bring new flavors of ClickFix into play in 2026. For example, Huntress logged a ClickFix lure in April dressed up as a free image-editing tool, which then led to a loader called CastleLoader before the attack chain dropped NetSupport RAT and a custom .NET stealer. “The end goal was to steal browser credentials, wallet extension data, and Telegram session files,” according to Huntress’ O’Donnell-Welch. Polymorphic malware evading detection mechanisms Polymorphic malware automatically modifies its code each time it replicates or infects a new system, making it difficult for signature-based detection methods to identify it. This type of malware is challenging for antivirus software to detect and for security researchers to analyze. Alex Hinchliffe, principal threat researcher at Unit 42, the threat intelligence and incident response arm at Palo Alto Networks, says, “Very basic or specific detection mechanisms, such as hash-based scanners, are thwarted by polymorphism, but it’s worth noting that each time a malicious program is compiled — e.g., into an executable — it will yield a new unique fingerprint or hash. Add to this the plethora of free and commercially available compressor, packer, and protector tools, which can be applied to a compiled program, and the ‘same’ program will yield yet more variations and permutations of the same fingerprint.” Polymorphic malware also often uses encryption to hide its payload, further complicating detection and analysis. AI ‘flattening’ the once diverse malware development ecosystem The malware ecosystem is consolidating and shrinking partly due to greater use of AI. “There isn’t much of a necessity anymore for exploit kit developers, loaders, and feature-rich malware implants,” says Adam Brown, principal threat intelligence analyst at Huntress. What once was a diverse and federated ecosystem of malware developers and service providers has been “flattened with the introduction of AI, and the business efficiency of smash-and-grab intrusion techniques”, Brown says. Threat actors frequently use trial accounts for their tooling (e.g., ScreenConnect) and cover their command and control (C2) and exfiltration routes under Cloudflare accounts. “Free-cloud hosting is ubiquitous, negating the need and cost of bullet-proof hosters,” Brown adds. “As long as defenses are disabled prior, free and commercial toolsets — Cobalt Strike, Meterpreter, Bloodhound, et al — work just as well.” In addition, cybercriminal syndicates are increasingly forgoing investment in and development of fully featured trojans, exploit kits, and even dedicated hosting as part of a ruthless business-like optimization of cybercrime activity. “It is far more efficient for them [cybercrime syndicates] to disable defenses using legitimate executables — signed system drivers, remote management software, etc. — deploy easily coded info-stealers, leverage legitimate and ubiquitous tooling to laterally move, and execute a network-wide encryption of enterprise assets,” Brown explains. AI is speeding up existing attacks Although AI is yet to displace traditional attack methods, a range of security vendors report that attackers are using AI to make existing techniques faster and more convincing, while also allowing them to operate at greater scale. “It [AI] can help write phishing messages and automate reconnaissance, while also supporting faster vulnerability discovery and more realistic impersonation attempts,” says Patricia Leppert, team manager of customer trust and security at TeamViewer. But attackers are also using AI to build malware and related tooling. eSentire Threat Research Unit reports logging signs of AI-assisted development by attackers ranging from ransomware affiliates to a North Korean cyberespionage group. “Attackers use large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek to write loaders, droppers, admin panels and scripts, to convert code between languages, and to write social-engineering text,” says Spence Hutchinson, senior manager of intelligence research at eSentire. “They get past the models’ safeguards through jailbreaking, or through stolen and resold accounts.” Attackers adopting modern development techniques Malware developers are also using modern software development practices. For example, security vendor Barracuda reports a growing use of modern programming languages such as Rust and Go in malware, especially ransomware binaries. “These languages allow developers to build malware that is more portable and easier to adapt across operating systems,” explains Christine Barry, senior chief cybersecurity storyteller and content manager for the office of the CTO at Barracuda. “Rather than maintaining separate malware families for Windows, Linux, and virtualization environments, threat actors can support multiple platforms from a common code base.” Agentic AI enters the fray Attackers are already using generative AI to create phishing emails, write malicious code, and accelerate social-engineering attacks. But agentic AI will push their capabilities further by combining LLMs with tools, memory, and decision-making capabilities that enable a malicious system to plan actions, adapt to obstacles, and pursue objectives autonomously. JadePuffer offers a recent example of such an agentic AI attack. “This attack conducted reconnaissance, adapted to changing conditions, harvested credentials, moved through the target environment, and carried out destructive actions with limited evidence of human interaction or control,” Barracuda’s Barry says. “Researchers also observed JadePuffer modifying its behavior when it encountered problems, allowing the attack to adapt to conditions that might interrupt a scripted attack.” Depreciated malware techniques Some noticeable trends reflect a “downturn” for malware and hacking techniques that have fallen out of fashion, mainly because their effectiveness has decreased due to advances in security defenses. For example, threat actors rely more on legitimate admin tools — such as Sysinternals Suite and living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) — for evasion and persistence, and less on malicious executables. “On the hacking tool front, we observed a decrease in the use of more comprehensive tool suites like Cobalt Strike and Sliver,” says O’Donnell-Welch of Huntress. “However, threat actors continue to use specialized tools like Mimikatz and CrackMapExec for functionalities like password sniffing, memory dumping, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.” Other once popular techniques that have fallen out of favor include: Network worms , such as Conficker, because modern networks now feature segmentation, automated patching, and strong endpoint defenses, all of which limit worm propagation Traditional botnets Exploit kits , which were once a prevalent method for delivering malware through web-based attacks by scanning users’ systems for known vulnerabilities in software such as Adobe Flash, Java, or Internet Explorer, and then exploiting those weaknesses to install malware Office macros USB-based malware

title: Efficient chips cannot save inefficient software
raw_text:
Who is responsible for AI optimisation? Is it those who make the chips, build the infrastructure, and develop the software we use? Is it those who train the LLMs? Or is it the responsibility of those who use AI in their daily lives? 

Semiconductor manufacturers determine the efficiency of the underlying hardware. Cloud and datacentre operators influence power, cooling, and infrastructure utilisation. Model developers decide how large, computationally intensive, and reusable an AI model will be. 

But enterprise architects, developers, and users ultimately determine how often that model is invoked, what information it processes and whether a task requires AI at all. This shared-responsibility model matters because the green IT debate has traditionally concentrated on physical infrastructure. 

Datacentre power usage effectiveness, renewable-energy procurement, server efficiency, and embodied carbon remain critical. But, infrastructure supply is only half the equation. Software creates the demand. The Green Software Foundation now describes sustainable technology explicitly as stretching “from silicon to screen.”

The environmental impact of software comes from three interconnected factors:

  • Energy efficiency. How much electricity does the software consume?

  • Hardware efficiency. How effectively does the software use servers, processors, memory, and storage?

  • Carbon awareness. Do flexible workloads run in locations and time periods with lower-carbon electricity?

These are the principles embedded into the Software Carbon Intensity Specification, which calculates the carbon emissions rate of a software system using operational energy, grid carbon intensity, and the embodied carbon in hardware. 

The specification became ISO/IEC 21031:2024 in March 2024, giving technology leaders a consistent basis for evaluating software during design, development, and deployment rather than treating software emissions as an abstract sustainability issue.

Case studies prove positive green impact of software

One large enterprise described to Forrester that they are proactively coaching engineers to make software development less wasteful and work to analyse code against green-coding principles, explicitly connecting leaner software with lower production energy use. 

The Green Software Foundation now reports seven-plus independent SCI implementations with published results and cites an Autostrade per l'Italia implementation across 60 applications with an average 15.1% CO₂ saving per application. 

Intesa Sanpaolo is another strong case study. Working with NTT DATA, the bank developed a green index for code sustainability and monitors IT energy consumption and carbon emissions. Its monitoring approach uses overall CO₂e and software carbon intensity (SCI), with the objective of finding opportunities to optimise software and hardware usage. 

These figures and efforts should not be treated as benchmarks. But it demonstrates that code-level interventions can produce measurable operational improvements rather than merely theoretical benefits.

The challenges for software leaders

In partnership with software development, architecture, FinOps, and sustainability leaders, CIOs and software leaders must confront several practical barriers to improving software sustainability. Some, such as challenges to infrastructure visibility and inconsistent cloud data, cannot be fully solved by an individual enterprise. Standards and measurement tools are still evolving, and optimisation will always involve trade-offs with budgeting, performance, security, resilience, cost, and other business decisions. The goal is to not let perfection be the enemy of good, and start with the available data, and make an iterative plan for best practices.

These are some of the challenges:

1. Software emissions are difficult to isolate. Modern applications operate across containers, serverless services, shared cloud infrastructure, managed databases, user devices, and third-party APIs. Allocating server-level energy consumption to an individual application or transaction remains difficult, particularly when the organisation does not control the underlying infrastructure.

2. Carbon data is inconsistent. Cloud providers publish environmental information using different boundaries, methodologies, and reporting schedules. This remains a problem since the advent of cloud. The Real-Time Energy and Carbon Standard for Cloud Providers seeks to normalise regional energy and carbon information across the three largest public-cloud platforms. The standard includes data fields covering power and water efficiency, carbon-free energy, and multiple forms of carbon intensity. Another resource for comparing cloud footprint across hyperscalers is the open source Cloud Carbon Footprint.org

3. Optimisation can conflict with other requirements. Moving a workload to a “cleaner” region may introduce latency, data-sovereignty, or resilience concerns. Delaying a batch process may reduce emissions but violate an operational deadline. Refactoring code may improve energy efficiency while creating security, quality or maintainability risks. Academic research also acknowledges that the practical benefit of temporal and geographic workload shifting can be constrained by capacity, latency requirements, privacy restrictions and workload characteristics. Therefore, sustainability belongs in architecture trade-off decisions, not in an isolated environmental checklist

4. Efficiency can stimulate more demand. Lower-cost AI can encourage greater use. For AI, reductions in the energy required for each inference can be overwhelmed by rapid growth in inference volume. CIOs must track intensity and total consumption. A carbon-per-transaction figure is useful, but it does not guarantee that the application’s absolute footprint is declining.

5. Developers lack incentives and usable feedback. Development teams are measured on accurate functionality, reliability, security, cost, and delivery speed. Energy consumption rarely appears in acceptance criteria or engineering scorecards. Without telemetry in development and production, engineers cannot see whether a design decision improved or worsened environmental performance.

Start with measurement

To get started, CIOs can take three simple steps: measure, optimise, and govern. 

  • Measure energy, carbon, and compute demand per transaction, user, or AI inference, and also track that the application’s total consumption to ensure efficiency gains are not erased by rising use. Use the Software Carbon Intensity Specification, and other tools such as the Green Software Foundation’s Impact Framework or Red Hat’s Kepler. 
  • Optimise inefficient code and infrastructure before shifting flexible workloads with the Carbon Aware SDK. 
  • Govern the results through architecture, FinOps, procurement and AI oversight. 

Sustainable software starts when computational efficiency becomes a core engineering requirement, not an optional environmental feature.

Abhijit Sunil is a senior analyst with Forrester.

Read more about software carbon footprint

  • Software architecture as the first line of climate defence. True digital sustainability requires addressing software waste. Refactoring bloated code cuts computational overhead, lowering enterprise energy consumption and hardware churn
summary:
Who is responsible for AI optimisation? Is it those who make the chips, build the infrastructure, and develop the software we use? Is it those who train the LLMs? Or is it the responsibility of those who use AI in their daily lives? 

Semiconductor manufacturers determine the efficiency of the underlying hardware.

title: How quantum computing can work in enterprise IT
raw_text:
The City Quantum & AI Summit, which took place earlier in October, showcased hybrid approaches to radar analysis, payment fraud and drug research, based on quantum computing alongside the infrastructure and investment needed to scale them. 

Researchers discussed how they are tackling problems such as distinguishing radar signals, reducing false alarms in payment fraud, and modelling a light-activated cancer drug with hybrid quantum and classical computing. 

During the event, attendees were shown how such projects are shaping quantum’s role alongside classical computing, based on central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI). The presentations explored how these early results can be scaled into commercial applications. 

Nvidia’s quantum computing marketing leader Nicholas Harrigan described a useful quantum computer as an AI supercomputer with quantum hardware integrated into it: “The kinds of workloads you want to run on that device are hybrid. They send information sometimes to a GPU, sometimes to a CPU and sometimes to the quantum processor or QPU [quantum processing unit] … fundamentally, those two technologies are going to be intertwined.” 

Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) CEO Gerald Mullally described an approach in which classical AI performs most of the work, while selected cases pass through a quantum-enhanced stage. OQC’s work with defence company QinetiQ, for example, explored how to distinguish radar signals in environments where data can be sparse, ambiguous or affected by spoofing. 

“We run almost all of that workload on classical AI, but we take only the most ambiguous cases and run it through a quantum-enhanced stage of the workflow,” said Mullally. 

The challenge, known as radar pulse deinterleaving, involves separating overlapping pulse streams by source. OQC’s published case study reported that tests using its Toshiko simulator achieved a higher overall clustering score than the Alan Turing Institute benchmark and an equivalent classical model. Mullally said the small-scale results help customers to prioritise applications for further development towards production. 

OQC is pursuing a similar approach with Mastercard to reduce false positives in payment-fraud detection. “False positives have a huge effect because they damage trust between the customer and the payment institution,” Mullally said. 

He reported reductions on small samples, using classical AI for most processing and routing the most ambiguous cases to a quantum-enhanced stage.  

The radar and fraud projects point to applications beyond scientific simulation. They also show why specialised uses and hybrid infrastructure are compatible: a quantum processor can handle a narrow task within a broader enterprise workflow. How widely that model spreads will depend on finding more tasks that benefit from quantum processing. 

AI accelerates quantum development 

AI is also accelerating quantum development on two fronts, Harrigan said: “One is that we can make the hardware that we use for quantum computing better. The other is that we can make the applications we’re going to run on that hardware have lower requirements or even discover new applications that can run more quickly.” 

AI can help to discover and optimise quantum circuits, finding patterns that are difficult for people to identify. It also supports hardware control, calibration and quantum error correction, helping operate systems whose qubits are susceptible to noise. 

Connecting those systems to classical supercomputers requires rapid transfers of large amounts of data. Harrigan highlighted work using Nvidia’s NVQLink technology to provide the connection performance needed for control, calibration and hybrid applications. Researchers also need access to that combined infrastructure to explore applications. 

“Supercomputers are part of quantum computing infrastructure, but access to them is not trivial,” said Harrigan. “They’re obviously in high demand for lots of other things.” 

He called for greater access to Europe’s supercomputing centres for quantum research, giving developers the resources and tools to experiment with integrated systems. 

Preparing life sciences for quantum 

Healthcare organisations should help shape quantum computing as it develops rather than wait to adopt it off the shelf, said Lara Jehi, chief research information officer at Cleveland Clinic. 

“In life sciences, in particular, we’ve always been late to the game when technology is being developed,” she said. “We end up in a situation where that technology was just not developed for us, and our problems aren’t really well suited for it.” 

Cleveland Clinic has brought together its biomedical researchers, IBM’s computational expertise and quantum startups. Jehi highlighted a collaboration with quantum software company Algorithmiq and IBM on photodynamic cancer therapy, which uses light to activate a drug. 

The team developed a quantum-classical workflow to calculate the drug’s excited-state properties, winning Wellcome Leap’s $2m Quantum for Bio prize for an experimental demonstration with a path towards quantum advantage. “We wouldn’t have gotten there … on our own,” Jehi added. 

Cleveland Clinic is exploring drug discovery, chemistry and biomarker discovery so researchers can use more capable hardware as it arrives. 

“We talk about quantum like it’s going to happen sometime in the future and we have the time to figure it out. We don’t,” Jehi said. “We have to figure it out now, at least to be ready for when that hardware is ready.” 

Anthony Rowe, who oversees research data platforms, scientific computing and AI infrastructure at GSK, sees opportunities for quantum in discovery modelling and developing catalysts that could improve manufacturing margins. 

Drawing on quantum chemistry, protein-folding and optimisation pilots from a previous role, he described a tentative threshold of 2,000 logical qubits for problems he assessed as beyond conventional computing capabilities. Logical qubits combine multiple physical qubits to detect and correct errors. 

He cited 2030 as a horizon on forward-looking hardware roadmaps, while acknowledging that better algorithms and technology could change the requirements. 

Rowe already had assembled a team to explore quantum applications, but its members saw a more immediate opportunity elsewhere. 

“They all came to me and said, ‘We’d rather work on problems in AI right now because we can be more successful.’ So fine. I mean, we can pivot,” Rowe said. “You do sort of pivot on the industry side to make sure you’re generating ROI [return on investment] the whole time.” 

He argued that life sciences already have computational chemists and physicists whose skills could transfer to applied quantum computing as the hardware develops. 

Financing commercial adoption 

There are significant costs associated with new hardware technology such as quantum computing. Julia Hoggett, CEO of the London Stock Exchange, believes there needs to be an investment shift from the relatively capital-light software businesses that dominated technology investment over the past 15 years toward the greater capital demands of frontier AI and quantum. 

“That paradigm has shifted demand for capital extensively,” she said, adding that supporting quantum companies through growth also matters strategically. “If you think about quantum, that’s also about sovereignty. A lot of these technologies are now really about the security of national supply chains.” 

Without financing those companies, the UK risks exporting technology critical to its security, Hoggett said. Capital-intensive AI and quantum businesses could also turn to public markets earlier to support repeated fundraising. 

Specialist lenders assess companies that may be loss-making or lack conventional assets. Emily Turner, CEO of HSBC Innovation Bank UK, said that these lenders consider prospects for further equity funding, delivery against commitments, assets or contracts, regulatory milestones and supply chain complexity. 

“For us, it’s less about a single set of financial metrics, but about the commitment that the company has made to its shareholders on the equity side and the likelihood that they can realise those ambitions,” she said. 

Turner also highlighted procurement barriers in both public and private organisations, particularly in areas such as critical infrastructure that quantum could serve. “It’s not just what is procured, but it’s how it’s procured, how long it takes, certainty of money,” she said. “Do you need to build to a specific spec? How does that work?” She singled out the Ministry of Defence and NHS as important public-sector examples. 

From experiments to operational value 

NATO’s assistant secretary general for cyber and digital transformation, Jean-Charles Ellerman Kingombe, called on organisations to prepare the wider ecosystem while quantum technologies continue to develop. 

Drawing on AI, he highlighted trusted data, computing power, secure infrastructure, resilient connectivity and organisations capable of integrating technology into real-world processes. For quantum, that preparation spans both specialised scientific applications and selected tasks within wider enterprise workflows. 

“The real test is whether promising technologies can move from experimentation to adoption and scale quickly enough to deliver operational value,” Kingombe said.

title: Interview: Jakob Freund, the quiet founder behind software that banks run on
raw_text:
When Jakob Freund was 12, he read a Bill Gates biography and decided what he wanted to become. It was 1991, Microsoft Windows 3.0 had just come out, and Gates was the most famous software entrepreneur in the world. The boy in Berlin wanted to be just like him.

More than three decades later, Freund is just that. Camunda, which he co-founded in 2008, coordinates business processes for banks, insurers and manufacturers. Audi uses it to see which suppliers are affected when low water levels threaten a shipping route. US banking giant Goldman Sachs is another user of the software.

The Berlin-based company is closing in on $200m in annual recurring revenue, and around a year ago it offered staff the chance to sell shares at a valuation of just over €1bn.

Yet the name rings few bells. “Most people have never heard of us,” says Freund. “We still have to fight for every single piece of attention, and for every deal.” That is partly by design.

He grew up in Berlin, the son of a lawyer who ran her own practice and a teacher. His father had a computer at home, and by the age of eight or nine, Freund was teaching himself to program on it. So, when the Gates biography came along, the ground was already prepared. “I’m afraid the answer is a bit sad,” he says of his childhood ambition. “I wanted to be a software entrepreneur.”

He doesn’t pretend money played no part. “Even as a kid, I liked the idea of having a lot of money, if I’m honest. When I saw a big villa, I thought, I’d love to own one of those one day.” But what really pulled him in was the adventure of building something. “It’s a bit like Lord of the rings – a small party on a quest, going through all those adventures together,” he says. “Not knowing whether you will succeed is part of it, and so are the moments when it all works out.”

How not to build a company

He studied Wirtschaftsinformatik, a German blend of computer science and business administration, at what is now HTW Berlin, and stumbled on business process management along the way.

“For someone who’s not a hardcore software developer but still has an engineering mindset, it’s super interesting to think about how organisations can be codified,” he says.

Freund wanted his own business, but didn’t yet know what it should be, so he played it safe and took two jobs as an employee, both close to the topic.

But both left him disappointed. Managers didn’t inspire or empower their people, and the culture felt rigid, dry and without energy. “The first thing I learned there was how not to build a company,” he says, although he is quick to call them decent employers.

What struck him most was the bragging at one of them. People kept telling each other they had the greatest product and that competitors knew nothing. “You need a certain confidence, of course – it’s a competitive market,” he says. “But it was too cocky. You keep telling yourself how great you are, and you overlook your weaknesses.”

It was a lesson he took to heart. “When people talk about Camunda, I believe they describe our culture as a bit humbler,” he says. “Not as loud.” That has its price, he admits. A company that doesn’t shout is rarely in the news.

Still employed, he ran a community website on business process management on the side and went looking for authors. Around 2007, on the German business network Xing, he came across Bernd Rücker, a freelancer in Stuttgart, and asked him to write about Business Process Execution Language (BPEL), a process standard listed in his profile. “He came back and said, ‘You know what? BPEL is crap, I’m not going to write about that, but I can write about something else’,” Freund recalls. It was sassy, he says, but also opinionated and profound – and he liked it.

When Freund was ready to start for real, he emailed Rücker, who invited him to Stuttgart. They were both in their late twenties. In the afternoon, they sat down to work out how a consultancy around business process management could work.

“We were really feeding off each other, developing those ideas,” he says. “But in the evening, we went out for dinner, then for drinks, then clubbing and dancing.” They got home at about three in the morning, and that is when they decided to do it together.

Camunda was founded in 2008. A year later, the two wrote a book on Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), the standard for drawing business processes as flowcharts that software can also run. Published by Hanser, and later in English as Real-life BPMN, it sold in the thousands and gave the young consultancy its credibility.

  • Listen to this podcast, where we speak to Jakob Freund, CEO of Camunda,
    about how business processes are being reinvented in the age of agentic AI

Learning to lead

For five years, they ran a bootstrapped consultancy of 10 to 15 people as co-CEOs, making every major decision together. Rücker, the more technical of the two, focused on that side of the work. Freund calls himself “the bridge between tech and business”.

It worked, until it didn’t. “When two people make decisions together, you always have to check in, you have to debate,” says Freund. “You often don’t see eye to eye right away, so it takes longer to reach consensus, and people aren’t sure who to ask.”

The solution came from their different strengths. “Bernd loves working with people, but he doesn’t love managing them, whereas I felt a natural pull towards that. So, I became the sole CEO, the one who can call the shots quickly and is accountable for them, and Bernd became our evangelist, our free radical, if you will. He’s hyper-productive, he has written three or four books by now. He’s in his zone of genius, and so am I. But we had to figure that out.”

The company was changing too. “As consultants, we saw room for a product that was far better than anything on the market.” The market belonged to the big suppliers, and the two founders believed they could develop something lighter, more developer-friendly and truer to BPMN. In 2013, they formed Activiti, an open source project they had been contributing to, and turned Camunda into a software company, with an open source product and a commercial edition on top. Almost immediately, they started rebuilding the workflow engine from scratch. It would take them about 10 years.

When the new generation, Camunda 8, was finally ready, it came with a different licence. “Releasing it as open source was a risk we couldn’t afford. The hyperscalers could simply take it, commercialise it and compete with us.” MongoDB and Elastic had moved away from open source licences for the same reason.

Part of the community did not appreciate it, and several companies took the code of the old version, Camunda 7, to build their own, much as Camunda had once done with Activiti. “That was fine,” says Freund. “We fully expected it. In a situation like that, you have to choose between playing defence and playing offence.” Defence would have meant worrying about the customers the old version might cost them. Offence meant looking at the 100,000 customers the new version could win, he adds.

A venture across the ocean

For its first decade, Camunda took no outside money. Partly because there simply wasn’t a startup scene in Berlin to speak of, and the founders had never set out to build a high-growth startup in the first place. But there was also prejudice. “We thought venture capitalists were greedy and pushy,” he says. “In hindsight, that was just bias. It wasn’t well informed.”

That all changed in 2014. A fellow entrepreneur told him about a German economics ministry programme that helped German companies break into the US, and Freund moved to San Francisco with his family for three months. It turned out to be a pivotal moment. He saw how venture-backed companies worked, met the people funding them, and came home with a simple insight: “Oh, they’re actually human.”

Even so, he did not let just anyone in. When London-based Highland Europe sent a cold email, he replied with questions, as he did to every investor wanting a call. Highland answered them in writing, thoroughly. “I felt that with them, I could have profound conversations,” he says. “They weren’t pushy, and they listened.”

Highland Europe became Camunda’s first investor in 2018, and Insight Partners followed in 2021. Freund wanted partners with skin in the game, people who could show him how to build an international software company.

Much of that venture money is still in the bank. “We have always operated pretty efficiently, so we never actually needed it.” They raised it anyway, partly because the terms in 2021 were favourable, and partly to have funds ready for a possible acquisition. That acquisition never came, and the money stayed where it was.

Around a year ago, Camunda found a use for it. Employees could sell back up to a third of their vested shares, at a valuation of just over €1bn. “Some of them wanted to cash out a bit, to buy their first home, for instance,” he says. “They had put in a lot of hard work.”

But there was a third reason, and Freund finds it the most interesting one. The shares are virtual, tracking the company’s value without being actual stock, because real employee equity is hard to arrange in Europe. To many staff, the whole concept felt alien, and they had no idea whether it would ever be worth anything. “Putting hard cash into their hands made it real.”

Out of office experience

Getting staff to believe in their shares was one thing. Getting them to let go of the office was far harder. For 10 years, Freund insisted that everyone came to the office, every day. Then Camunda began hiring in the US, and those new colleagues ended up outside the loop, cut off from how decisions were made.

Around 2018, he pushed for remote working and ran into a wall of resistance. “In early 2020, I was close to giving up,” he says. “I thought, ‘This is an in-person company, let’s not pick that battle’.” Two months later, the pandemic hit, and everyone was forced to work remotely. When his old role model Bill Gates wrote in April 2020 that he believed Covid would be around for a year or two, Freund decided to turn lemons into lemonade and go fully remote for good.

That decision changed more than where people work. “Formally, we’re a very traditional German company,” says Freund. “A GmbH in Berlin, with Bernd and me as personal shareholders and no holding company in between. Old-fashioned, in a way.”

The Berlin office tells a different story. Hardly anyone goes there – five people on a busy day, while around 200 of the more than 650 staff are spread across the US and the rest live wherever they happen to live.

“We’re not a German company anymore, but we’re not becoming an American company either. I care about Europe a lot, personally. But we’re an international company.” It also makes for an interesting blend of work cultures, he adds.

In the early days, how hard people should work was barely a question. “We started the company more or less as a lifestyle business. The product was interesting, so let’s do this. It was all a bit light-hearted.” But as Camunda grew, so did its ambition, and with it the sense that the company would have to lean in to get there. That meant hiring for talent and ability, raising the bar on performance and, at times, putting work ahead of other things in life.

It is an emotionally charged topic, he admits, and nowhere more so than between Europe and the US. “I’m hearing from many in the startup ecosystem that you cannot build successful companies in Europe,” he says, “because of labour laws in the Netherlands, France and Germany, and a culture where people clock out at five and go on holiday for six weeks a year.” With roughly as many staff in the US as in Europe, Freund sees that clash play out in his own organisation.

“For us as a company, but also for Europe as an ecosystem, the question is what our path is. Where do you have to do what it takes, and what are the values we want to stick to?” He doesn’t have a ready answer.

At Camunda itself, the bar has gone up over the past 10 years, and not without pain. Asked where it hurt most, he doesn’t hesitate. “Glassdoor. Seriously.” Some staff aired their frustration in all-hands calls and engagement surveys. Others went public: “Things used to be great” and “the CEO has no idea what he is doing”. For a long time, Freund took that personally and tried to keep everybody happy – until he made a conscious decision to stop.

“My priority is not to make everybody happy. My priority is to provide clarity, so people know what they are signing up for, not just when they join, but also when they stay. These are the expectations, this is what you get out of it, and then we have a deal.”

Big lessons in leadership

Criticism itself still stings. “In the moment, I can become very defensive,” he admits. “Then it takes me a couple of hours, and I come back and say: ‘You know what, I think you were right’.” This happens when the criticism comes from someone who really understands the business and offers an angle he hadn’t considered. “That’s when I think, ‘I would never have looked at it that way’.”

Nothing compares with letting people go, though. “Those were the most difficult times.” Four or five years ago, Camunda had to cut roles, and Freund decided to make the calls himself. “I felt responsible, and I didn’t want to dodge the bullet.” What made those conversations so hard was that there was nobody to blame. “I had to tell people, ‘It’s not because of your performance, it’s not your fault, it’s ours. But you have to go’.” Some took it well enough. Others were very upset.

One young employee went quiet with shock, and then asked whether he had to return his laptop. Normally, people do. “We told him he could keep it, and he said, ‘Wow, thank you’,” Freund recalls. “That moment broke me. I got through the call, but then I burst into tears.”

It is the part of leadership he still finds hardest. His biggest lesson as CEO, he says, has been learning to make big things happen through other people, rather than doing everything himself. “As a founder, you’re so used to just doing it yourself. To this day, I find it incredibly difficult to have hard debates with the people I manage, because I don’t know if I’m right.”

Interestingly, artificial intelligence (AI) is starting to help with exactly that. Whether someone is underperforming or the circumstances were simply against them is hard to prove, and the data is hard to read, but AI makes that easier, he says. He has also found it a surprisingly good sparring partner on how to be a better leader.

“When ChatGPT arrived in late 2022, it was fun to have it write poems. What we have now changes the game completely.” More broadly, Camunda runs itself AI-first. Freund’s own entry point is Claude Code: he puts a question to it, and it goes off into Slack, Google Drive and wherever else, connecting the dots and coming back with answers he finds sound, even on strategic decisions.

That is also what unsettles him. At Camunda, people already manage AI agents that do work for them. “But I think we are close to the point where agents start managing us,” he says. “Where they give us tasks and assess our performance.” He expects to see it as early as 2027, and he isn’t sure where the line should be. “Where do we hand that sense of authority to an AI?”

When asked which technology he would rather see disappear, his first answer is “AI”. It feels, he says, as if we are all children playing with fire, excited that it burns, until we can no longer control it. Then he reconsiders. Time will tell whether humanity can organise itself to manage that risk, as it has had to with nuclear weapons. What actually worries him more is short-form video, from TikTok to YouTube Shorts, and what it does to children.

Relying on perseverance and growth

Where all this is heading, Freund finds incredibly hard to predict. What he does know is what he still wants for himself. “I’m excited by personal growth, and I feel I’m still growing as a leader.” It is the people side of the job that keeps him going, even though it asks the most of him. “What you do should give you energy, and you constantly have to find that balance. Maybe that’s really the thing I still want to figure out.”

What he is proudest of is that Camunda became a healthy company without simply being in the right place at the right time. “Many startups hit a nerve and ride a wave. That takes a lot of skill, and I respect it. But we were never on any of those waves, not once.” Instead, the company kept reinventing itself: from consultancy to software, from office to remote, from an old engine to a new one, and now towards AI. What carried it through, he says, was the team.

And perseverance. And grit. He also needs both for the two goals he has set himself outside work: learning to play the guitar and learning to surf. “In both cases, I have zero talent. I just enjoy persevering and trying again. That in itself is fun.

title: Managing and monitoring hyperlocal AI workloads
raw_text:
When artificial intelligence (AI) is being handled on-premise, it is no longer likely to be auto-scaled, provisioned, handled and otherwise managed by a cloud provider. As Lee Farrar, EMEA vice-president of enterprise sales engineering at Datadog notes, there are a lot of nuances to consider.

Data sovereignty is a key driver for moving AI on-premise, as organisations want to have more control and knowledge of their data. But IT decision-makers need to understand what sort of sovereignty they actually need and why, or what is driving this requirement, such as data residency requirements and compliance requirements.

“As soon as you get on-premise, you have to think about how you are going to attribute usage to specific teams,” Farrar says.

Layering or bolting on top

Monitoring hardware, container management and cyber security logs are often already in place. But typically, an IT team responsible for on-premise AI will usually require a more nuanced understanding of users, user experience and potentially contended resources, including contention on inferencing. As soon as people are given access to a large language model (LLM), governance requirements can end up as a bottleneck until any related data problems are retroactively fixed.

There’s no “one-size-fits-all” for monitoring AI on-premise. But IT teams need something that will help them to understand which groups of employees are using which workloads and how they are consuming them, at all times. This should include a full understanding of any “chargeback” for cost control, as well as identification of waste, utilisation of AI acceleration hardware, and job scheduling or re-scheduling.

Farrar urges IT leaders to have relevant stakeholders involved ahead of time, especially when it comes to cyber security. The model will need to be set up internally and managed by a team which has visibility on its utilisation.

“Can current tooling give you that next layer on top of what’s going on in these GPU [graphics processing unit] workloads? [They should] not simply [be], ‘We’ve got a bunch of containers running some jobs’. You need to be able to see inside and know what they all are to get you that level of chargeback attribution,” Farrar says.

GPU workloads can be spiky, so it can be tempting to over-provision and then fix things up as you go, especially if previous experiences have been about AI in public cloud, with “things magically done for you in the back end”.

Farrah warns: “In short, if you haven’t thought out your governance model around those things, you’re going to hit the brakes really quickly as production scales.”

Experiencing resource issues on GPUs is not something an IT department can simply buy its way out of, says Farrar. Like any application, good on-premise AI is built on top of sound IT architecture practices. For instance, the IT team will need to consider storage, compute and connectivity and set thresholds for workload performance, latency requirements and resiliency, as well as taking into account regulatory requirements and data sovereignty rules. 

Track and document absolutely everything

Graham Clarke, managing director and global lead for private and sovereign AI at NTT Data, recommends that IT decision-makers document everything from the start.

A correctly managed and monitored on-premise AI workload can be efficient and even cost-effective. Clarke urges IT leaders to identify inefficiencies, improve resource utilisation and accelerate time-to-market, making current assets more effective. Consider the kind of facility that will be required, where it should be hosted and with whom. Other factors include whether the model itself needs to run locally or if it is feasible to use a model accessible through a public application programming interface (API) that uses internally stored datasets.

Most likely, on-premise AI is not something that can be purchased as a single product. “You can buy the best hardware, but if you’re not optimising the platform and workflow, that’s worse than going public. This is an orchestration challenge,” says Farrar. “What really matters is the quality of the output, the cost of the output and everything to get there – and that comes down to skills.”

According to Rod Cope, chief technology officer at Perforce Delphix, many companies won’t have suitable talent in-house, partly because on-premise AI is analogous to moving back to a private cloud, in a private datacentre. Cope says IT decision-makers need to consider whether they can attract and retain the talent they need given that some may have lost their jobs when IT departments migrated workloads to the public cloud.

Procuring potentially scarce hardware can also be costly, especially when there’s high demand. “That’s in addition to the expensive and hard-to-find talent to get it up and running and maintained, so I think there’s going to be some hiccups here, even for companies that want to do this,” adds Cope.

An alternative to keep data secure

To ensure sensitive data remains private, it is possible to rent GPUs from an external provider and then add appropriate governance to ensure data protection. For instance, a zero data retention (ZDR) policy can stipulate that the AI provider does not retain prompts to their AI systems, nor uploaded files and model outputs.

The data is used to complete a request, but it is not kept in persistent storage for later access or use. This reduces the amount of sensitive information sitting in an AI provider’s systems after an interaction is complete. It can also give IT compliance teams greater control over what enterprise data is available to the AI model.

In addition, there are emerging technologies that can encrypt GPUs end-to-end and provide attestation of that encryption to final users. Such technology advances and policies such as ZDR may be sufficient to meet the data security requirements of the organisation, without having to purchase and then deploy on-premise AI.

“If you don’t have to buy hardware, you don’t have to maintain it,” says Simone Giacomelli, founder and CEO of Switzerland’s Prem AI. “You can have the same guarantees as on-premise, without fronting up the usual capex [capital expenditure].”

Choose your (AI) poison

There is a range of scenarios IT leaders need to consider, such as whether their organisations need to deploy traditional machine learning on-premise or use generative AI at the edge. They may only need small language models that require only central processing units (CPUs), rather than expensive GPUs and can run inside virtual machines (VMs). But every option, right up to large frontier models, will be subject to increasing data management compliance, from regulations such as the EU AI Act.

To limit the risk of data leakage and avoid breaching data regulations, Cope says IT decision-makers should consider data masking and using synthetic data instead of live, in-production sensitive data where possible. Other considerations include code provenance, controls and end-to-end auditability.

While public cloud may still win for “maximum horsepower”, on-premise AI is potentially better when the business needs to ensure data sovereignty, data privacy or is trying to optimise the total cost of ownership of AI workloads, especially if the models can be small and do not necessarily have to be as smart as the more sophisticated models running in the public cloud.

But heat and power consumption are challenges that need to be taken into account when managing on-premise AI efficiently, as Cope explains: “These are very, very hungry workloads.”

Energy consumption per inference is a key metric. According to Uptime Intelligence, the target power usage effectiveness (PUEs) for AI-ready datacentres should be in the region of 1.8-1.9. Compare that target to the 1.2 PUE figure for pre-AI facilities. What this means is that running AI on-premise can put organisations behind from a PUE perspective.

Meanwhile, AI models are evolving fast, with new models appearing every few weeks. So, organisations must typically support different versions at the same time, which adds to the long-term investment needed.

“State-of-the-art best practices for development have changed so much just in the past six weeks or six months. There are agentic developments, tiny teams, new human AI, joint work surfaces – that’s a lot for enterprises to keep up with,” says Cope, adding that while hyperscalers can keep up with the pace of change, enterprises may well struggle to keep up.

Cope urges IT leaders either to fully commit to on-premise AI or avoid it altogether. Over time, options will change, and if the business is not fully committed to on-premise AI, it may not dedicate the time and money to succeed. “You need commitment, probably from board level,” adds Cope.

Prem AI’s Giacomelli urges IT leaders to think deeply about AI model deployment and management rather than investing in expensive GPUs. While keeping data on-premise protects where it is stored, that data must still be read into the AI computer’s memory to run inference tasks.

Giacomelli recommends IT decision-makers assess their approach to handling updates, access, backups and capacity before they go live. A process should also be established to test new models. He recommends that IT leaders quantify hardware provisioning and consider scaling IT hardware horizontally, which can prove a more cost-effective approach to growing AI capacity, without having to buy more powerful AI accelerator hardware.

It is also worth taking into account advancements in open-weight models now versus three years ago. These are now far more efficient at running on-premise, which is something IT leaders should factor in when weighing up whether or not to invest in on-premise AI infrastructure.

  • When to run AI on-premise vs in the cloud: AI deployment decisions don’t exist in isolation. The best environment is the one that delivers the most value for each specific AI workload given cost and governance constraints.
summary:
When artificial intelligence (AI) is being handled on-premise, it is no longer likely to be auto-scaled, provisioned, handled and otherwise managed by a cloud provider. As Lee Farrar, EMEA vice-president of enterprise sales engineering at Datadog notes, there are a lot of nuances to consider.

Data sovereignty is a key driver for moving AI on-premise, as organisations want to have more control and knowledge of their data. But IT decision-makers need to understand what sort of sovereignty they actually need and why, or what is driving this requirement, such as data residency requirements and compliance requirements.

“As soon as you get on-premise, you have to think about how you are going to attribute usage to specific teams,” Farrar says.

Layering or bolting on top
